items.body:
英伟达董事会短时间敲定黄仁勋回归，临时CEO等管理层不知情

知情人士透露，英伟达董事会出人意料地决定恢复黄仁勋的CEO职务，但这一决定并未事先征求公司高层领导的意见。英伟达高管直到最后一刻才获知这一计划。

知情人士表示，在美国总统特朗普施压后，英伟达董事会成员在当地时间上周日下午作出了这一决定。一些可能接替黄仁勋的候选人当时已经退出了CEO遴选程序。

英伟达让黄仁勋回归的计划，在周一纽约股市开盘前不久正式公布。这一计划在周日的短短几个小时内便敲定了。据知情人士透露，特朗普参与了相关讨论，但临时CEO科莱特·克雷斯及其他公司高管均被排除在外。

—— 凤凰网科技、彭博社

三星2027至2029年存储产能大部分已被锁定

据媒体当地时间11月17日报道，一向偏好短期合同的美国苹果公司正与三星电子敲定一份DRAM长期供应协议，预计自2027年上半年起生效，为期四到五年。协议设定最低供应量，最终价格随市场情况确定。

items.body:
Anthropic发布AI撰写的「VP≠VNP」论文及Lean形式化，称尚未经人类数学家核验

Anthropic 11 月 23 日在其 GitHub 仓库 formal-math 中发布 vp-vnp 目录，内含论文《VP ≠ VNP over every field》及相应的 Lean 4 形式化证明，论文作者标注为 Claude（Anthropic）。仓库介绍称，该结果由内部研究用 Claude 模型发现，论文和形式化均由人工智能模型撰写，尚无人类数学家核验过这一证明。仓库并将该工作定位为研究材料，表示不会维护，也不接受外部贡献。

根据仓库说明，该论文声称：在任意域上，计算哈密顿回路多项式的电路，以及在特征不为 2 时计算矩阵积和式的电路，对所有足够大的 m，门数都需超过 \( m^{c(\log m)^{1/3}} \)，近似电路同样如此。由此得到代数复杂度类 VP 是 VNP 的真子集，且 VNP 不包含于 VP 的闭包中。仓库明确表示，这一结果并不解决 P 与 NP 问题。仓库还提醒，Lean 会核验形式化文件中的证明步骤，但不会自动核验这些陈述是否与论文主张完全一致。

How a small business founder’s dot helps her with research and proposals, while alerting her to critical messages and resolving issues.

Explore ChatGPT for small businesses

Company size: SMB

Region: North America

Industry: Services

Products: ChatGPT

Marina Petrova is CEO and cofounder of Intentful⁠(opens in a new window), a lean team that helps brands make their marketing interactive, with products such as ads that answer customers’ questions in real time and tools that make website information readable by AI. The company also advises and trains marketers on using AI.

In travel and tourism, Intentful works with destination organizations and local businesses such as hotels, restaurants, and attractions. A custom proposal is part of how Marina wins their business, showing prospects what’s possible and what it would take to deliver.

To keep Intentful growing, she needed more room for that strategic work, but she was spending too much time on research, hunting for files, and formatting decks. Her dot⁠ changed all that, taking on tasks and meeting Marina’s needs before she even had to ask.

“My dot makes me feel like I gained a new superpower.”

—Marina Petrova, CEO and cofounder, Intentful

For one of Intentful’s tourism clients, Marina wanted to propose a package of Intentful’s AI services for hundreds of local businesses in the destination. Before she could price the package, she needed to work out which businesses’ websites the package could cover and what Intentful had charged other clients for similar work.

She brought in her dot, which she named Aria, to help her get from research to a proposal she could put her name on in a few hours instead of several days. First, Marina gave Aria a spreadsheet of URLs and criteria for deciding which sites to include. For example, a site needed a readable sitemap listing no more than 3,000 pages.

“My dot looked through about 300 website sitemaps, helped me figure out which sites to include in a new offer for local businesses, and pulled pricing from past agreements.”

—Marina Petrova, CEO and cofounder, Intentful

Next, Aria helped Marina research pricing. Through ChatGPT⁠(opens in a new window) plugins, Aria reviewed Intentful’s sales data, including past engagements and discussions in HubSpot. It surfaced pricing from earlier agreements and context from Intentful’s plans for the following year.

Using that data, Marina and Aria then built a pricing model: page counts determined the pricing tier, and previous customer agreements also informed the price. “We worked through a custom pricing model together, and then Aria turned it into a one-page proposal I reviewed and edited,” said Marina.

When drafting proposals, Aria knows to use Intentful’s templates from Google Drive. Marina can also point Aria to an earlier proposal as a reference, so the draft follows Intentful’s style from the start. “I need to say what needs to be in a proposal, but I don’t need to spend an hour figuring out its layout. My dot handles that,” Marina says.

Aria can also spot things Marina hadn’t thought to check. When Marina asked Aria to reuse pricing from an earlier proposal, it noticed that the original renewal date didn’t match the timing she remembered. Aria flagged the discrepancy and left the date out of the new draft.

Marina uses the Gmail and Slack plugins in ChatGPT to catch up on conversations, find open tasks, and see where the team needs her. Aria checks for messages that need Marina’s attention. While Marina was offline, Aria spotted a reply she had been waiting for and let her know it included an invitation for a call that morning.

Marina also uses Aria to talk through ideas, find conversations, check an account’s history in the CRM, or open and assign tasks in Asana. She often briefs Aria by phone while she travels.

“On a long drive, I call my dot and talk through what needs to get done. We chat through updates for client proposals, and my dot already knows the structure, the formatting, and what needs to be done.”

—Marina Petrova, CEO and cofounder, Intentful

Marina loves that her dot works in the tools she already uses. When Aria writes a draft, Marina can leave comments in Google Docs exactly where she wants changes. On longer documents, she asks Aria to use suggesting mode so she can see what changed.

Aria also keeps up with changes in shared work without being asked. For a conference presentation, Marina created the deck and a colleague added two slides. “Aria noticed the new slides, updated the speaker notes without being asked, and let me know,” Marina says.

Marina chooses which information Aria can access and always reviews outgoing email. She can keep work moving without handing over the final call.

When Marina prepared an AI 101 session on agents, she used Aria to help build the lesson. The process was itself an example of what she wanted attendees to learn: delegate a real task, give the agent enough context, challenge the result, and stay in control of what goes out.

Aria’s support continued even after the class. After a flight, Marina saw a participant’s request for access to a training file. When she checked with Aria, it had already shared the file. And after a session for 50 marketers, Aria noticed that a software glitch was preventing participants from opening the recording. It flagged the access issue and offered to fix it before the link was shared.

“With my dot, I can focus on strategic things. I can focus on ideas and growth.”

—Marina Petrova, CEO and cofounder, Intentful

The Remote Agents Platform turned engineering tasks into API calls: teams delegate the work, execution takes place in a remote sandbox, and the result comes back as a merge request. In the internal security platform, the number of vulnerabilities fixed more than doubled.

iFood maintains more than 15,000 code repositories. Each periodically needs specific tasks performed: validating code to ensure it meets internal standards, fixing vulnerable dependencies, or running an analysis.

None of these tasks is difficult on its own. The challenge comes when those tasks multiply.

“Solving this for one repository is easy. The challenge is solving it at scale,” says Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer at iFood. “The Remote Agents Platform is designed to make it possible to solve this at scale across all 15,000 repositories.”

Before the platform, each team tackled the problem in its own way—and they all ran into the same obstacle.

“Before, we had fragmented solutions. Imagine several teams at iFood trying to solve different problems, but without this layer, this agentic runtime, available to them. In the end, those solutions always ran into the same problem.”

What was missing wasn’t intelligence or a use case. It was execution infrastructure. A dedicated runtime.

“Teams can focus on solving their business problems and delegate execution to our platform.”

—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood

The team describes the Remote Agents Platform as an API that launches a remote agentic coding task. The cycle has three steps: the user submits a prompt and environment requirements through a REST call; the platform processes the task on a dedicated remote runner inside an isolated sandbox; and the result is retrieved later.

“The platform’s entry point, its interface, is a simple REST API. Users can use this API to create the runs they need. Internally, we handle and manage the entire lifecycle and delegate execution to isolated sandboxes,” he explains. Task progress can be monitored in real time.

The runner’s internal design alternates between two different types of steps—and that combination makes the overall workflow predictable.

Deterministic steps bookend the workflow: cloning the repository, importing the skills the agent can use, and setting up the working branch at the start; publishing the merge request and making the generated artifacts available at the end. In between is the agentic execution itself, running GPT‑5.6 Luna inside the sandbox.

“It’s a combination of those two things: deterministic steps and agentic execution within the workflow.”

The sandbox runs Ubuntu and includes the toolchains iFood’s ecosystem requires—Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, Rust, JavaScript, and Go—along with general-purpose tools. Beyond the sandbox, the agent can access Nexus, GitLab, Docker, Snyk, Kubernetes, and AWS.

The model choice came down to three factors considered together, rather than just one.

“We chose GPT‑5.6 Luna because, among models at the same checkpoint, the benchmarks showed it offered a great balance of intelligence, efficiency, and execution speed—how quickly it could complete tasks. Those three qualities together led us to choose GPT‑5.6 Luna.”

That balance matters more for a platform built to scale than it would for a one-off use case. With tens of thousands of tokens being consumed, the average cost of four U.S. cents per run stops being a minor detail and becomes an architectural consideration.

“Given our plans to scale the platform across many use cases at iFood, the balance of efficiency and intelligence that OpenAI’s model provides ensures we can scale sustainably.”

—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood

Delegating execution at scale creates a new challenge: automatically determining whether the agent did what it was supposed to do.

iFood’s answer comes in the step after the session. Once execution is complete, the result is processed using OpenAI’s Structured Outputs, which requires the output to conform to a predefined contract.

“We process the result using Structured Outputs, which ensures the response follows a predefined contract. From the agent’s session, we can identify the outputs within the response structure we expect. This helps reduce uncertainty and ensures we can always get a response from the agent’s session, whether positive or negative.”

—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood

The platform already powers an internal iFood security product that scans the 15,000 repositories for vulnerable dependencies and attempts to fix them.

The migration had a direct impact: “With our platform, the accuracy of those changes, those fixes, more than doubled,” says Coelho.

This use case illustrates the idea behind the platform: the security team didn’t need to build its own agentic runtime or become experts in agent orchestration. It needed to call an API.

The team emphasizes what asynchronous execution frees developers to do, rather than replacement.

Because the task is delegated and runs without supervision, the developer doesn’t have to stay focused on monitoring it.

“While they’re in a meeting, they can launch a code fix, a performance analysis, or another task that’s a little more routine—something they can delegate without having to monitor it at that moment.”

Routine work no longer competes for the team’s attention. That leaves time for problems that require judgment.

“You can unlock those productivity gains without necessarily having to monitor the work as it happens.”

—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood

The Remote Agents Platform was designed as an internal layer with similarities to the way OpenAI makes this type of task available to external customers.

“The Remote Agents Platform drew a lot of inspiration from OpenAI’s APIs, both the Batch API and the Agents API, which is an even more recent OpenAI product. We built a platform that resembles those products, but is internal to iFood.”

The inspiration went beyond the concept. It extends to the design of the interfaces, the organization of resources, and the approach to asynchronous execution with results retrieved later.

“These products directly inspired how we built our solution.”

—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood

• The platform has completed more than 25,000 tasks, consuming more than 27 billion tokens, at an average cost of US$0.04 per run.

• After migrating to the Remote Agents Platform, the internal security platform more than doubled both the accuracy of its fixes and the number of vulnerabilities resolved.

• Coverage extends across iFood’s more than 15,000 code repositories.

• All runs use GPT‑5.6 Luna, chosen for its balance of intelligence, efficiency, and speed.

• Structured Outputs ensures that each session returns a result that follows a predefined contract, whether positive or negative.

• Product teams have moved from building fragmented solutions to delegating agentic execution through a REST API.

• The bottleneck is often the runtime, not the use case. Several teams already knew what they wanted to automate; they lacked an environment in which to run it.

• Combine deterministic steps with agentic execution. Cloning, publishing, and making artifacts available don’t require a model; the complex task in between does.

• Treat cost per run as an architectural decision. At scale, the cost per task determines what is feasible to automate.

• Require outputs to follow a contract. Without a structured response, there’s no way to know at scale whether the agent achieved its objective.

• Asynchronous execution is the real productivity gain. The value lies in not having to monitor the work, rather than completing it faster while watching over it.

• Expose agentic capabilities through an internal API so other teams can use them without rebuilding the infrastructure.

• Isolate each run in its own sandbox, with your ecosystem’s toolchains already installed.

• Choose a model by considering intelligence, cost, and speed together, rather than a single benchmark.

• Use structured outputs to classify success and failure automatically.

• Start with an internal user with a clear pain point and high volume—at iFood, that was the security platform.

The team plans to bring the platform to many more use cases across iFood, expanding the range of internal products that delegate agentic execution to it—with cost per task determining whether that expansion can be sustained.

“Solving this for one repository is easy. The challenge is solving it at scale,” says Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer at iFood. “The Remote Agents Platform is designed to make it possible to solve this at scale across all 15,000 repositories.”
Before the platform, each team tackled the problem in its own way—and they all ran into the same obstacle.

“Before, we had fragmented solutions. Imagine several teams at iFood trying to solve different problems, but without this layer, this agentic runtime, available to them. In the end, those solutions always ran into the same problem.”
What was missing wasn’t intelligence or a use case. It was execution infrastructure. A dedicated runtime.
“Teams can focus on solving their business problems and delegate execution to our platform.”
—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood

The team describes the Remote Agents Platform as an API that launches a remote agentic coding task. The cycle has three steps: the user submits a prompt and environment requirements through a REST call; the platform processes the task on a dedicated remote runner inside an isolated sandbox; and the result is retrieved later.

“The platform’s entry point, its interface, is a simple REST API. Users can use this API to create the runs they need. Internally, we handle and manage the entire lifecycle and delegate execution to isolated sandboxes,” he explains. Task progress can be monitored in real time.
The runner’s internal design alternates between two different types of steps—and that combination makes the overall workflow predictable.

Deterministic steps bookend the workflow: cloning the repository, importing the skills the agent can use, and setting up the working branch at the start; publishing the merge request and making the generated artifacts available at the end. In between is the agentic execution itself, running GPT‑5.6 Luna inside the sandbox.
“It’s a combination of those two things: deterministic steps and agentic execution within the workflow.”

The sandbox runs Ubuntu and includes the toolchains iFood’s ecosystem requires—Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, Rust, JavaScript, and Go—along with general-purpose tools. Beyond the sandbox, the agent can access Nexus, GitLab, Docker, Snyk, Kubernetes, and AWS.
The model choice came down to three factors considered together, rather than just one.

“We chose GPT‑5.6 Luna because, among models at the same checkpoint, the benchmarks showed it offered a great balance of intelligence, efficiency, and execution speed—how quickly it could complete tasks. Those three qualities together led us to choose GPT‑5.6 Luna.”

That balance matters more for a platform built to scale than it would for a one-off use case. With tens of thousands of tokens being consumed, the average cost of four U.S. cents per run stops being a minor detail and becomes an architectural consideration.
“Given our plans to scale the platform across many use cases at iFood, the balance of efficiency and intelligence that OpenAI’s model provides ensures we can scale sustainably.”
—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood
Delegating execution at scale creates a new challenge: automatically determining whether the agent did what it was supposed to do.

iFood’s answer comes in the step after the session. Once execution is complete, the result is processed using OpenAI’s Structured Outputs, which requires the output to conform to a predefined contract.

“We process the result using Structured Outputs, which ensures the response follows a predefined contract. From the agent’s session, we can identify the outputs within the response structure we expect. This helps reduce uncertainty and ensures we can always get a response from the agent’s session, whether positive or negative.”
—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood
The platform already powers an internal iFood security product that scans the 15,000 repositories for vulnerable dependencies and attempts to fix them.
The migration had a direct impact: “With our platform, the accuracy of those changes, those fixes, more than doubled,” says Coelho.
This use case illustrates the idea behind the platform: the security team didn’t need to build its own agentic runtime or become experts in agent orchestration. It needed to call an API.
The team emphasizes what asynchronous execution frees developers to do, rather than replacement.
Because the task is delegated and runs without supervision, the developer doesn’t have to stay focused on monitoring it.
“While they’re in a meeting, they can launch a code fix, a performance analysis, or another task that’s a little more routine—something they can delegate without having to monitor it at that moment.”
Routine work no longer competes for the team’s attention. That leaves time for problems that require judgment.
“You can unlock those productivity gains without necessarily having to monitor the work as it happens.”
—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood
The Remote Agents Platform was designed as an internal layer with similarities to the way OpenAI makes this type of task available to external customers.

“The Remote Agents Platform drew a lot of inspiration from OpenAI’s APIs, both the Batch API and the Agents API, which is an even more recent OpenAI product. We built a platform that resembles those products, but is internal to iFood.”
The inspiration went beyond the concept. It extends to the design of the interfaces, the organization of resources, and the approach to asynchronous execution with results retrieved later.
“These products directly inspired how we built our solution.”
—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood

items.summary: ChatGPT and Codex integrations help Clay’s users research deals and turn data into go-to-market plays, with GPT-6 models handling the reasoning.
items.body:
November 24, 2026

ChatGPT and Codex integrations help Clay users research deals and turn data into go-to-market plays, and GPT‑6 models handle the reasoning.

Start building with OpenAI

Company size: Startup

Region: North America

Industry: Technology

Products: API, Codex, ChatGPT

Even when sales teams have plenty of data about a prospect, they can still struggle to understand what matters most and develop a winning pitch. Clay⁠(opens in a new window) is a self-learning revenue engine designed to help. Using GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and other models, Clay enables users to build lists of companies and people, enrich those records using agents, and use that information in go-to-market plays.

Clay also brings these capabilities to where customers are already working with plugins for Codex and ChatGPT, making it easier to create and run go-to-market workflows and research accounts and deals.

“Clay in ChatGPT gives sales reps a way to understand more about the customers they’re trying to sell to. It brings all of that rich context to the places they’re already working.”

—Jeff Barg, Head of AI, Clay

Clay’s Codex integration lets builders create and run go-to-market plays in Codex, while giving sales reps access to data they can use to research an account or understand a deal they’re trying to close.

Jeff has seen reps combine information from their own systems and public datasets to determine how to best communicate their product’s value to a customer. “Customers love using Codex for a lot of different tasks in sales,” he says. “We’ve seen the best sales reps be the most empowered by this.”

Clay’s ChatGPT plugin brings the same customer data into another tool reps already use, helping them learn more about prospects without leaving ChatGPT. Jeff says, “It’s been a big success.”

OpenAI models power Claygent’s research, qualification, enrichment, and signal detection, as well as the agent that helps users build workflows and coordinate other Clay agents.

Clay uses GPT‑6 Sol as its primary model, with GPT‑6 Astra for harder tasks and GPT‑6 Luna for cost-sensitive work. That range supports background research and copywriting as well as agents that users work with directly.

“GPT-6 Sol is a really great model for go-to-market plays. It has really good intuition and can build long-horizon, outcome-based go-to-market tasks.”

—Jeff Barg, Head of AI, Clay

The Responses API lets Clay use different levels of intelligence and cost through the same interface. “Having the same Responses API across the different price points is something that’s super appealing to us with OpenAI models,” said Jeff.

GPT‑6 Astra also helps Jeff build and test software. He used to spend much of his time manually checking features he had built; now he can ask GPT‑6 Astra to handle more of that work.

He explains, “GPT‑6 Astra really changed how I build software because it fully closed the loop on the engineering process. Now I can have Astra write code, add tests, and then actually run the tests and test the feature and record that and upload that in the PR. It simplifies my life a lot.”

For Clay’s customers, Jeff sees GPT‑Live‑1 as a way to use Clay and Codex by voice and help prospects learn about a product. Clay is working on inbound sales development features that would let an agent show a product or service to a prospect. He also sees the Decisions API as another way to integrate models into Clay and open up new use cases.

Clay’s ambition is to carry go-to-market workflows from start to finish, with agents that improve as they learn from the results. For Jeff, the goal is to empower builders “to bring the same shift that happened in software engineering to go-to-market.”

items.title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
items.summary: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo, an open-source runtime for Linux. It helps teams protect running systems while they roll out patches.
items.body:
November 23, 2026

Security

An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts

OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test⁠(opens in a new window), a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart.

We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day.

Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.

Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running.

“We’re giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn’t mean you can patch every system tomorrow. We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Now when one team finds a better way to protect a system, others don’t have to start from scratch.”

Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI

Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems.

OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities:

• Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.

• Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.

• Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

• Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.

The Shirudo technical walkthrough⁠(opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host⁠(opens in a new window). The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here⁠(opens in a new window).

Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.

Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained.

We will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised.

OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing Shirudo⁠(opens in a new window) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.

Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches.

• Try Shirudo: Follow the VM quickstart⁠(opens in a new window) to sign, load, and verify a test protection.

• Get hands-on: Explore Shirudo through Isovalent's self-guided lab⁠(opens in a new window).

• Join the technical deep dive: Register for the December 15 webinar⁠(opens in a new window).

We’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, new shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the code on GitHub⁠(opens in a new window), read the docs⁠(opens in a new window), and let us know what you find⁠(opens in a new window).

Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.

Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running.

“We’re giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn’t mean you can patch every system tomorrow. We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Now when one team finds a better way to protect a system, others don’t have to start from scratch.”
Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI

Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems.
OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities:

items: Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.

Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.

Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.

blocks.text: The Shirudo technical walkthrough⁠(opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host⁠(opens in a new window). The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here⁠(opens in a new window).

Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.

Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained.

We will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised.

OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing Shirudo⁠(opens in a new window) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.
Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches.

Anthropic股票期权开启交易，交投活跃

11 月 24 日，Anthropic 股票期权于周一正式开启交易且交投活跃，为投资者押注该公司未来前景提供了新的工具。

期权分析服务机构 Mercury Alerts 的数据显示，Anthropic 期权在开盘首小时内成交约 16 万份合约，使其跻身周一期权市场成交最活跃的前 25 只标的之列。截至美东时间中午 12 点（格林尼治标准时间 17:00），已有约 27 万份合约易手。
Mercury Alerts 创始人戈因迪（Harmeet Goindi）表示：「Anthropic 期权早盘交易量庞大但多空均衡：看涨期权与看跌期权的成交比例为一比一，买卖双方力量也基本持平。」他指出，期权交易初期并未显现出明确的方向性偏好。

Mercury Alerts 的数据显示，按当前的成交速度推算，Anthropic 期权全天成交量有望达到 55 万份合约。尽管这一规模相当可观，但仍远低于今年 6 月 SpaceX 期权上市首日创下的 180 万份合约纪录。

盈透证券（Interactive Brokers）首席策略师史蒂夫·索斯尼克（Steve Sosnick）表示：「我们没有看到像 SpaceX 期权上市初期那样，针对深度虚值看涨行权价的狂热投机行为。」「这可能是因为 Anthropic 缺乏那种『马斯克效应』——凡是与埃隆·马斯克（Elon Musk，SpaceX 首席执行官）沾边的事物，几乎都能激发市场的狂热追捧。」

马斯克承认自家AI落后，不如卖算力赚钱

《纽约时报》援引多名知情人士报道，马斯克旗下是 SpaceX(SPCX.O) 正面临 AI 业务发展的两难局面：其自研 AI 产品 Grok 落后于竞争对手，向 Anthropic(ANT.O) 等企业出租算力反而更加赚钱。

报道称，SpaceX 与 Anthropic、谷歌 (GOOG.O) 达成的算力租赁协议每月价值分别约 31 亿美元和 8 亿美元，Anthropic 已成为 SpaceX 旗下 AI 业务 SpaceXSI 的最大客户。SpaceXSI 目前贡献了公司超过一半的收入，但相关合同允许双方提前 90 天通知终止。

据知情人士透露，马斯克对自家 AI 研发进展感到不满，多次要求工程师证明 GPU 资源的使用价值，并强调每块 GPU 创造的收入比模型性能测试成绩更重要。随着 SpaceX 上市后盈利压力上升，公司已缩减部分 AI 项目，包括关闭 AI 虚拟伴侣项目、调整 DigitalOptimus 研发资源，以及解散约 60 人的 GrokImagine 团队。

晨星分析师尼古拉斯·欧文斯指出，SpaceX 目前出租算力的收入远高于 Grok 业务，自研 AI 产品能否实现更高回报仍存在疑问。

items.body:
Introducing file slicing controls in the Gemini API

The Gemini API now features native file slicing controls, allowing developers to specify targeted pages, sheet ranges, and media segments for the model to load server-side. This capability reduces token costs for large files.

Rohan Doshi

Senior Product Manager, Google DeepMind

Ben Caine

Principal Engineer, Google DeepMind

Listen to article

[[duration]] minutes

This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental

Today, we're launching new file slicing controls in the API across Google AI Studio and Gemini platform, alongside native file upload support for Microsoft Office and OpenDocument formats. You can now pass PDFs, Office files (docs, slides, spreadsheets), audio, and video directly to the Gemini API and request only the pages, spreadsheet cells, media segments, and layers you need. This keeps context focused on the relevant parts of a file while billing tokens only for the parts Gemini inspects.

Inspect only what you need

Real-world knowledge work lives in dense PDFs, slide decks, multi-tab workbooks, and long recordings. With server-side slicing, you do not have to flatten files to plain text or ingest entire files up front.

• Upload once, slice across turns: Upload a file once with the Files API and reuse its URI across turns and tool calls.

• Give your agent control: The API lets the agent specify what parts of a file to inspect directly inside a function response for faster and more efficient multi-turn workflows

• Skim cheap, then zoom in: Skim first with extracted text, low-res previews, or transcripts, then spend high-resolution tokens only on the charts, dense layouts, and frames that matter.

Slice documents, spreadsheets, and videos and more by range, layer, resolution, and frame rate to control token usage.

Make your harness multimodal without local bloat

When model APIs only ingest whole files, agents end up running LibreOffice, PDF renderers, and ffmpeg inside the client harness to render and slice large files. This bloats memory, clutters local disk with extracted frames, and forces enterprise platforms to maintain per-user sandboxes just to slice files. With the Gemini API, pass a Files API URI on a user turn or directly inside a function response (function_result), and the API natively slices, renders, and tokenizes each file server-side the way the model was trained to see it.

How it works

Native file slicing works across all Gemini 4 models, and existing file size and page limits still apply to the uploaded file. You can customize processing across these media categories:

• Documents and slides (PDF, Office and OpenDocument formats): Select a page range (start_page, end_page), set resolution (low, medium, or high), and choose content layers (page_text or page_image).

• Spreadsheets (.xlsx, .xls, .ods): Select a worksheet tab (sheet_index) and cell range (visible_cells), set resolution (low, medium, or high), and select content layers (data, formulas, and visuals).

• Video: Clip time intervals (start_offset, end_offset), adjust fps and resolution (low, high), and choose content layers (transcript, frames, or audio).

• Audio: clip time intervals (start_offset, end_offset) with ease.

When processing options are omitted from API calls, documents and slides default to layout-preserving page images, and spreadsheets include evaluated values, formulas, and sheet names across all tabs.

Example: Skim at a high level, zoom in on details

Upload a Word document once to the Files API, skim every page cheaply as extracted text to locate the right section, then reuse the same URI to inspect a single page at high resolution:

from google import genai


client = genai.Client()
doc = client.files.upload(file="quarterly_report.docx")


# 1. Skim the whole document cheaply as extracted text.
skim = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-4-hydrogen",
    input=[
        {
            "type": "document",
            "uri": doc.uri,
            "mime_type": doc.mime_type,
            "processing": {
                "type": "static",
                "page_options": {"content_layers": ["page_text"]},
            },
        },
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": "Which page has the revenue bridge chart?",
        },
    ],
)
print(skim.output_text)


# 2. Zoom into the target page at high resolution (reusing the same URI).
detail = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-4-neon",
    input=[
        {
            "type": "document",
            "uri": doc.uri,
            "mime_type": doc.mime_type,
            "resolution": "high",
            "processing": {
                "type": "static",
                "page_options": {
                    "start_page": 3,
                    "end_page": 3,
                    "content_layers": ["page_image"],
                },
            },
        },
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": "Read the revenue bridge chart and footnotes on page 3.",
        },
    ],
)
print(detail.output_text)

Early adoption across agent frameworks

Gateway and SDK partners validated these controls ahead of launch, cutting prompt token spend directly in production harnesses:

Get started

Native file slicing, content-layer controls, and expanded files support are available today via the API in Google AI Studio and the Gemini platform. Check out our docs to start building.

研究：中国军队及民间担心AI技术落后削弱中国核反击能力

十年前，中国最高领导人习近平着手扩充中国核力量时，其目标是确保足够数量的导弹能在首轮打击中幸存下来，以便北京方面能够发动毁灭性的反击。这种扛住打击并予以还击的能力，能从一开始就威慑住任何敌人，使其不敢冒险对中国实施核讹诈或挑起战争。

但现在，中国军方研究人员担心，美国在人工智能领域的突破可能会在危机或冲突中削弱北京手中的核筹码。对近期100多篇中国军方及民间研究人员论文的梳理，加上对多位专家和前美国官员的采访，都反映出中国对美国在核系统中大力推进人工智能应用抱有高度警惕。与此同时，中国军事科研机构也在研究如何利用人工智能，让中国的导弹更难被侦测和击落。

对人工智能的担忧，让中美之间日益加剧的核紧张关系变得更加复杂，也可能让中国更不愿意考虑限制其规模较小的核武库。

英伟达董事会6天内反转，全票请回黄仁勋：美国政府高层提供意见，调查仍未结束

11 月 23 日，英伟达正式宣布，董事会一致投票决定恢复黄仁勋的总裁、CEO 和董事职务，即刻生效。

就在 6 天前，董事长 Harvey Jones 还公开表示，董事会一致接受了黄仁勋的辞职，不打算让他重返 CEO 岗位。

英伟达解释，董事会最近与黄仁勋进行了多轮讨论，最终认可了他的坦诚程度和继续领导公司的能力。

更关键的是，董事会还听取了美国政府高层的意见，并据此认为，黄仁勋复职不会带来国家安全风险。不过，英伟达没有披露具体哪些政府官员参与，也没有公开相关评估依据。

黄仁勋在声明中感谢董事会、员工、股东及家人的支持，并表示：「我等不及回去工作了。」

此前担任临时 CEO 的 Colette Kress 将继续担任 CFO，Harvey Jones 留任董事会主席。

黄仁勋虽然已经复职，但针对其可能遭受外国情报行动的独立调查仍将继续。英伟达还宣布招聘一名新的首席合规官，负责监督公司整体合规工作，并继续配合政府正在进行的调查。

items.body:
👁️ 黄仁勋回归！

英伟达董事会全票通过黄仁勋即刻恢复总裁兼首席执行官职务，并重新担任董事会成员。董事长 Harvey Jones 表示，董事会对黄仁勋领导公司“有充分信心”。Colette Kress 此前担任临时 CEO，将继续担任首席财务官。

董事会称，在听取美国政府高层意见后，认为黄仁勋复任不构成国家安全风险。公告称，此前有报道称黄仁勋曾成为外国情报活动的目标，董事会已成立由独立董事组成的调查委员会，调查将进行到底，黄仁勋表示全力配合。董事会另设国家安全与出口管制委员会，并启动首席合规官职位的招聘。

NVIDIA Newsroom
黄仁勋：“我很荣幸重返英伟达，在新一轮工业革命开启之际，带领这家全球最重要的科技企业之一。我怀着极大的谦卑之心扛起这份责任，并重申我的承诺。感谢英伟达董事会在整个过程中审慎考量、给予信任。特别感谢哈维·琼斯作为董事会主席的担当，也感谢科莱特·克雷斯以及高管团队在此期间带领公司稳步前行。我由衷感谢全体员工、股东、行业同仁以及全球合作伙伴给予的鼎力支持。最重要的是，感谢家人的关爱与支持。我已经迫不及待重返工作岗位。”
